| 515 | DELBLOCK.1 — the delete that scrubbed first and failed second | **No migration** (mig 538, applied today, supplies the catalog function this leans on). `DELETE /api/contacts/[id]` ran two **irreversible** steps before the one that can fail: `redactWhatsAppForContact()` (wipes `wa_phone`, `wa_profile_name`, message bodies, media URLs) then `redactInBodyForContact()` (**hard-deletes** the InBody rows), and only then `DELETE FROM contacts`. Two foreign keys reject that delete outright — `person_groups.primary_contact_id` (RESTRICT, NOT NULL) and `offer_purchases.contact_id` (NO ACTION; the same FK violation, differing only in deferrability) — so for any contact holding either, the operator got the contact still present, its WhatsApp history scrubbed, its InBody scans gone, and a raw Postgres message on screen. **Measured against prod 2026-08-12: 892 of 8,578 contacts were undeletable — 887 via `person_groups`, 6 via `offer_purchases`** — and it was fully reachable from the UI until IMPACTCAT.1 (mig 538) landed hours earlier, because the dialog's `block_delete` bucket was always empty so it happily offered the confirm box. Same shape as the merge bug fixed the same day (mig 533): **a destructive act sequenced ahead of an operation that can fail, with nothing to roll it back.** The fix asks what blocks the delete BEFORE touching anything, via `getContactImpact()` → `public.contact_delete_impact` (mig 538) — **derived from `pg_constraint`, deliberately not a hand-listed pair of tables**, which is the anti-pattern migs 533 and 538 exist to remove and which would go stale the day a third RESTRICT lands. Non-empty `block_delete` → **409** with `{ success:false, error, data:{ block_delete } }`, naming the rows to reassign, having performed **no scrub and no delete**; 409 rather than 400/500 because the request is well-formed and authorised and it is the resource's current state that forbids it. **It also fails CLOSED:** `partial: true` means the catalog RPC was unavailable or a count errored, and on that path the legacy 21-pair fallback answers — which can never populate `block_delete` at all, so an empty list there proves nothing. Partial (or an unexpected throw) therefore **refuses with 503**, retryable, rather than guessing: a refused delete is recoverable by clicking again, a half-scrubbed contact is not. The auth + location guards still run first, so an unauthorised caller learns nothing about the row. **The existing 500 is KEPT as a backstop and that is not belt-and-braces:** the check and the DELETE are two statements, not one transaction, so a `person_groups` row inserted in between still reaches the database — the guard narrows the window from "892 contacts, every time" to "a concurrent insert", it does not close it. Closing it properly means one server-side function like `merge_contacts()`; **explicitly NOT done here** (see the PR's Found-not-fixed). `ContactEditDeleteActions.jsx` renders the 409 as the blocking rows plus "Nothing was deleted or redacted" — the impact fetch that opened the dialog is a snapshot and can be stale by click time, so a 409 is reachable with an empty `Blocking` section on screen and must not read as a generic failure. DELETE is now registered in `src/lib/openapi.js` for the first time (200/401/403/404/409/500 + 503). Tests pin that the scrub mocks were **never invoked** on every refusal path, not just the status codes. |
| 514 | BRIDGE-UNDELIVERED.1 — the bridge that is reading fine and cannot deliver (mig 537) | **Migration 537 — WRITTEN, NOT APPLIED.** Closes the last gap from the 12 Aug bridge incident. Mig 531 began storing `ble_bridges.last_pending_samples` — the bridge's local flush queue at the last heartbeat — and **nothing graded on it**, though its own COMMENT names the fault: a queue that climbs and never falls means the bridge is READING straps fine and cannot DELIVER them (network path down, token rejected, `/samples` erroring). That is a **third** failure distinct from the two 531 covered, and the only one every existing signal actively certifies as healthy: heartbeats keep arriving, `status` stays `online`, `last_seen_at` stays fresh, radios report ready — while champ-bridge's 5,000-sample buffer (`src/buffer.js` MAX_BUFFER) fills and then **drops the oldest sample per new one**. **The marker exists because the count has no history:** `last_pending_samples` is a whole-column overwrite, so one reading of 3,200 is indistinguishable from a healthy bridge mid-flush and from an hour stuck — "climbs and never falls" is not derivable from it. `pending_stuck_since` records the start of the current unbroken run of non-empty reports; a time-series table would be a prune, a retention decision and a second source of truth about bridge health for a **one-bridge** fleet, so the transition is persisted, not the stream (same call as 531 denormalising the adapter flags, and as `fleet_device_health` existing at all). **Semantics are asymmetric on purpose:** `pending_samples === 0` **clears** unconditionally and is the only thing that can (a bridge that drains even once is never left looking stuck); `> 0` **arms only if NULL**, as its own `.is('pending_stuck_since', null)` UPDATE so Postgres does the compare-and-set in one statement — a read-modify-write would race, and re-stamping on every heartbeat would reset the clock so it could never age into a grade; **no telemetry touches nothing**, the same rule the mig-531 columns follow, or a pre-531 bridge would either invent a backlog or have a real one silently wiped. The marker write is best-effort and logged: the heartbeat has already succeeded, and failing it would make the bridge look OFFLINE — a missed alert turned into a fake outage. **`undelivered` needs THREE conditions, not one.** (1) `pending_stuck_since` older than **10 min**: the flush loop runs every 3s, so that is ~200 consecutive failed attempts, and no benign event has that shape (a reboot is ~90s); it is also the floor the 5-minute cron can observe at all. Against the deadline, time-to-first-drop is `5000 / (straps × 1Hz)` — 16.7 min at 5 straps, 27.8 at 3, 83 at 1 — so 10 min plus ≤5 min of cron latency lands **before** the first drop at the occupancies this studio runs (the BRIDGE-BLIND.2 measurement found only 17 of 84 classes had any strap). **Stated rather than papered over: a full 30-strap room fills the buffer in 2.8 min, which no 5-minute cron can beat.** (2) `last_pending_samples ≥ 1000` — **LOAD-BEARING**, and the reason time alone is not the test: a healthy bridge is nearly always mid-cycle, so its queue reads ~90 at any instant and can be non-zero at *every* heartbeat of a busy morning, holding the marker open for hours. 1,000 is champ-bridge's `SERVER_BATCH_CAP`, exactly what one successful flush POST clears, so the queue has failed a whole round trip's worth of delivery; ordinary accumulation would need >333 straps against a room capacity of 30. (3) a **fresh `last_telemetry_at`** — the marker is only ever written by a heartbeat, so a bridge that stops reporting leaves a frozen timestamp that gets older by itself and would look worse every 5 minutes forever off one stale claim. **Precedence: below service_down, above adapter_down and blind.** Those two say "no data is being produced"; this says "data exists and is being lost on a clock", and they co-exist happily — ranking a standing radio fault first would let a box report ADAPTER for weeks while its other radio's readings drained away. It cannot outrank service_down because "is it talking at all" must be settled before reasoning from a marker only heartbeats write. No flip-flop against adapter_down (unlike blind, this does not alternate with the class schedule); quiet overnight like both, since the studio is shut and the 04:00 reboot clears the buffer anyway. **Copy states the observation and the consequence and guesses no cause** — network, rejected token and a 500 from us are indistinguishable from here, and naming one sends the operator to the wrong place: *"bridge online and reading straps, but it reports 2,400 samples it has not been able to send for 12 min. It can hold 5,000 before it starts dropping the oldest, so heart-rate data will begin to be lost."* — becoming *"That is its whole 5,000-sample buffer, so it is already dropping the oldest readings to make room."* at capacity. Mig 537 also widens `fleet_device_health_state_check` a third time (**ordering dependency: a state the CHECK rejects fails the upsert for the WHOLE tick, losing every device's de-dup memory and re-alerting on everything next tick**), and `FleetAdmin`'s `STATE_CHIP` map gains `undelivered`/`adapter_down`/`blind`, which it had never been given — all three were rendering as neutral slate. **🔴 KNOWN, AND IT SHIPS DARK FOR A SECOND REASON:** champ-bridge only heartbeats `if (pendingCount() === 0)` (`src/index.js`), so on today's bridge software a heartbeat carrying `pending_samples > 0` **essentially cannot occur** — the marker will never arm and this grade cannot fire until champ-bridge sends telemetry regardless of queue depth. A delivery failure currently surfaces (late, and mislabelled) as `service_down`, because the suppressed heartbeats stale out `last_seen_at`. The CRM half is deliberately built to be correct **and** robust to that gate being lifted — which is what conditions (2) and (3) are for. Not verified against a live bridge. |
| 513 | EMAIL-MERGE.1-6 — two tickets that are one conversation, folded reversibly (mig 536) | Follows #512. The 12 Aug incident left **two tickets for one Dublin City Council conversation**, the operator replied on both, and the council received the same answer twice. Nothing could join them. A merged ticket is a **TOMBSTONE — `status='closed'` plus `merged_into_id`, deliberately NOT a fifth status value**: a new enum would have to be audited through every view filter, the count endpoint, the mobile status picker and the needs-reply badge, and this estate has been bitten by exactly that. `scopeToUnmerged()` hides them from **one shared place** (list + count), applied in the list's BASE query rather than inside `applyView` — a per-view filter is one the next view forgets. **Reparenting is not cosmetic:** the inbound webhook threads replies via `email_inbox_messages.ticket_id`, so without repointing it a later council reply would land back on the dead ticket. **Write order is load-bearing** (no cross-statement transaction): reparent → target counters → tombstone LAST, so a crash leaves messages moved and the source live-but-empty, which is re-runnable; stamping the tombstone first would hide a ticket whose mail never moved, i.e. silent loss. **`merged_from_ticket_id` on the messages is what makes unmerge exact** — keying the restore on `ticket_id` would drag the target's own native messages across, and the round-trip test seeds a native message specifically to catch that. **Chains are refused so exactness holds by construction:** `canMerge` already refused tombstones, but a SURVIVOR is not a tombstone, so A→B→C re-stamped A's rows and quietly broke the reversibility promise — merge now also refuses a ticket that has ABSORBED a previous merge (query for any message with a non-null stamp; **a failed lookup is 500, not "none"**). **`unread_count` cannot be recomputed from rows** — it is a counter (`increment_email_ticket_unread`, zeroed by `…/read`), so the tombstone RETAINS its count as the receipt of what the survivor absorbed and unmerge subtracts it back, clamped at 0; everything else is rebuilt by a new pure `ticketFieldsFromMessages()`, which clocks on `created_at` because an inbound `sent_at` is **the sender's own Date header** and a remote clock could otherwise seize the queue. Both tickets go through `loadTicketForUser` (#1266) on POST **and** DELETE; refusals 404, lost race 409. **A tombstone stays READABLE** so a bookmark, a push link or Undo still lands somewhere useful — which opened a hole: the reply route gates on `loadTicketForUser`, which knows nothing of merge, so a reply from a tombstone would reach the member and be filed where no queue shows it, *the duplicate-reply failure wearing the feature's own hat*. Guarded **server-side** in reply and forward (409 + the survivor id), not only in the UI: mobile has no merge concept at all and ships a reply button. Compose is exempt, verified rather than assumed (it mints a new ticket). Notes are refused too, deliberately — a note on a hidden ticket is one the operator loses silently. **Cross-mailbox merge is permitted but is a readership change**: mig 502 keys message RLS on the ticket's mailbox, so folding `accounts@` into `studio@` makes billing mail readable by studio-only grantees; the confirm step now says so plainly, naming both mailboxes. `merged_by` is left **unindexed on purpose** — an audit stamp nothing filters on; indexing it would trade an `unindexed_foreign_keys` INFO for an `unused_index` INFO plus write cost, and `released_by` on two sibling email tables is treated the same. Merge and unmerge are audit-logged (`email_ticket.merged` / `.unmerged`) since DELETE nulls `merged_by`, which would otherwise leave no record a conversation moved twice. **Known limits:** the picker lists open+pending only (reopen a closed duplicate first); `status`/`closed_at` are not restored by unmerge; two operators merging the same pair in OPPOSITE directions simultaneously can tombstone both (each stamps a different row, so no PostgREST condition can catch it — only a trigger could; recoverable by unmerging either, documented in the route). **Not device-QA'd; jsdom only.** |
| 512 | EMAIL-PARTICIPANTS.1-10 — a reply reaches everyone on the thread, and the thread says who they are (mig 534) | Operator-reported: an inbound from `eleanor.brennan@dublincity.ie` landed on the ticket whose requester is `ratesoffice@dublincity.ie`. **The threading matcher was correct** and must not be "fixed" — her `References` named our 09:10 send to `ratesoffice@`, because the rates office forwarded our mail to her internally and Outlook carried our Message-ID down the chain. Dropping recipient 26 quietly is the same defect in a new costume. **(4) Sticky removals** (mig 534, `excluded_participants text[]`) via `PATCH …/participants`, gated **inside `loadTicketForUser`** (#1266 — a per-route check resolves at the caller's *active* location) with 404 refusals. **The exclusions apply to the requester fallback too**, or removing the requester would appear to work and then undo itself on the next send; an emptied audience refuses rather than mailing someone the operator took off. Review found the composer still *showed* the requester as a chip in that state while the route 400s, and that removal was a **one-way door** — the copy said "restore one to reply" with no restore control anywhere — so removed participants now render as struck-through chips outside `RecipientEditor` (everything inside that box means "goes to") with a restore action, and both writes serialise (read-modify-write on one column). **(5) The thread reads like a mail thread**: real From/To/Cc per message, **Bcc always at top level, never behind the collapse**, live participants in the header with "Opened by" shown only when the counterparty has moved, and `<address> joined this thread` markers — suppressed on the opening message, whose addresses are still *consumed* so nobody is announced later for having been there from the start. **(6) Contact linkage is now the From address or nothing.** The webhook took `contact_id` from the `email_sends` row named by a **sender-supplied** header before ever reading From, so a stranger who was forwarded our mail was written onto the member's record. Mobile gets the real audience read-only (removal stays web-only), closing the 08-09 finding that its footer claimed one recipient while every reply is reply-all. **EMAIL-PARTICIPANTS.12 — three contradictions a whole-branch review caught that per-task review did not.** **(a) `to[0]` silently stopped being the live counterparty the moment we answered.** The lead was `newest.from_email` unconditionally, and on an OUTBOUND newest message that is one of OUR addresses, dropped a line later by `exclude` — so the order reverted to first appearance and the set flipped from `[eleanor, ratesoffice]` to `[ratesoffice, eleanor]` on the reply. Web's placeholder, mobile's footer **and the `Opened by` divergence marker** all key on `to[0]`, so the marker built to announce a changed counterparty vanished on the reply to the very ticket it existed for. The newest message is now read both ways — inbound: its From; outbound: its first **To** (never a Cc) — recognised from `direction` (added to `PARTICIPANT_COLUMNS`; `bcc_emails` still is not) *or* from the From being one of `exclude`, either signal sufficient. | 491 | EMAIL-FORWARD.1 — staff can forward one message off a ticket to somebody else | **Migration 501** (`forwarded_from_id` on `email_ticket_attachments`, `forwarded_message_id` on `email_inbox_messages`, and `recalc_email_storage_usage` rewritten to count a shared object once). The last item on the ticketing list, and it sits on top of the four features that landed the night before: `resolveRecipients()`/`toPostmarkFields()` (the 25-cap, the case-insensitive dedupe, the own-address exclusion, the Bcc guarantee), `sendTicketEmail()` (the ticketing Postmark server, `email-send` stream, mailbox From with a sender-signature fallback), and the inbound + outbound attachment machinery. Nothing in those was reimplemented. **WHERE IT LIVES: an outbound message on the SAME ticket**, carrying `forwarded_message_id`. A ticket of its own would split one issue across two queue rows, neither carrying the other’s context; on the ticket, the accountant’s reply threads straight back through the ordinary inbound path (Reply-To is the mailbox, the Postmark MessageID is on the row). The thread shows an ordinary outbound bubble plus a “Forwarded the message from …” marker read off the COLUMN, never off the “Fwd: ” subject prefix — a subject is editable text, and a renderer that pattern-matches it is one rename away from lying. **THE TICKET IS DELIBERATELY NOT TOUCHED** (no status, no `last_message_*`, no `first_response_at`): `needs_reply` is `open AND inbound last message`, so stamping an outbound one would have dropped a ticket the member is still waiting on out of the queue because somebody asked the accountant about it. That breaks the one-row-one-object assumption in three places and all three are handled: the recalc counts shared bytes once (mig 501), the prune takes only OWNER rows as candidates, and after a batch is marked it CASCADES the mark to every row pointing into it — without a second decrement, since a reference row was never charged. Without the cascade a forward would have become a chip that downloads a 404, silently, months later. **THE CAP IS A CHOICE, NOT A TRUNCATION.** 25 MB can arrive inbound; 7 MiB may leave. The composer lists every forwardable file with a checkbox and a running total, pre-ticks the lot when it fits and pre-ticks NOTHING when it does not (a greedy subset would be files the operator did not decide to leave out), and the server refuses an over-budget set naming both numbers. A row with `storage_path` NULL is listed with its reason and is not selectable — hiding it would have staff telling a member they never sent it. Every refusal is pre-send: nothing sent, nothing written. **BCC.** Two leak directions, both closed. As a recipient: a forward derives NOTHING from stored correspondence (the addresses are typed), and the source SELECT does not name the column. In the quoted body — the new one, and the natural mistake — `forwardedHeaderLines()` is a CLOSED list of five (From, Date, Subject, To, Cc); Bcc is ABSENT rather than redacted, because “Bcc: (hidden)” still tells the recipient somebody was blind-copied. So `text_body` is quoted and escaped by the same `textToHtml` the reply uses: the markup never becomes markup, which is stronger than sanitising it. The recipient is told formatting was dropped; the full original stays on the ticket. **Internal notes cannot be forwarded** — 400 in the route, hidden in the thread. A note was sent to nobody and is written assuming only colleagues read it. **No `email_sends` row** (a forward goes to a third party — one against the member’s `contact_id` would put “we emailed you” in their own history for mail they never received); delivery status is unaffected, mig 498 stamps `email_inbox_messages` by `postmark_message_id` directly. Every address is written to `audit_events` under the sender’s name, like a compose rather than a reply. Mobile is OUT: no new permission key, and picking recipients and files off a quoted message is a desk task. Registered in `openapi.js`. **Migration 501 is written, NOT applied.** |
| 490 | EMAIL-OUTBOUND-ATTACH.1 — staff can attach files to a ticket reply and to a new email | **No migration** (checked: `email_ticket_attachments`, the `email-attachments` bucket and `add_email_storage_bytes` already carry everything an outbound row needs). Attachments shipped **inbound-only** — a member could email us a photo and it stored, previewed and downloaded, but there was no file input anywhere in `src/components/tickets/` and no attachment handling in either send route. It was in the original spec ("cc/bcc, replies, attachments") and only half landed; Richard found it trying to send a test email with a file. **THE BYTES NEVER GO THROUGH VERCEL.** A request body over ~4.5 MB is rejected with a 413 *before* the handler runs — the same platform limit that forced the inbound Edge shim — so a multipart POST carrying a 6 MB attachment to `…/reply` would fail with none of our code running. The browser therefore uploads each file **straight to the private bucket** and the send request carries only `{ draft_id, index, filename, mime }` (a few hundred bytes): the repo's existing three-step signed-upload shape, now its fifth user (card receipts, contractor invoices, WhatsApp template media, landing-page media). **THE CLIENT NEVER NAMES A PATH** — not "the path is validated", never accepted. `POST /api/email/attachments/upload-sign` *builds* `outbound/<caller's profile id>/<draft_id>/<index>.<ext>` from the session and mints a one-shot token for exactly that key; the send route **re-builds the identical key** from the same inputs. A client that lies about the mime derives a different extension, the object is not there, and the send is refused — it cannot reach another key. Because the caller's own profile id is a path segment, the worst a staff account can address is its own drafts: never another person's, never the canonical `<location_id>/…` half of the bucket, never the shim's `inbound/…` half, never up a `../`. **The upload gate IS the send's gate** — `ticket_id` runs `loadTicketForUser` (location + `email_inbox` there + the mailbox must be visible), `mailbox_id` runs the compose route's send-as check, now extracted verbatim into `_helpers.js` as `loadSendingMailbox()` and shared by both, because two copies would be two definitions of who may send as `accounts@`. 404 never 403, as everywhere on this surface. **SIZE: 7 MiB of raw file bytes per email, derived not guessed.** Postmark's own support article (art. 1056, read 2026-08-07) says "Total message size, including attachments, can be **10 MB**" and "We calculate the size of the email **after** it has been base64 encoded" — so the constant is the *decimal* 10,000,000 (the smaller reading, which can only ever be conservative) and `base64Bytes(7 MiB) = 9,786,712`, leaving 213 KB for a 10,000-char body sent twice, the signature, the subject and the MIME scaffolding. Enforced **server-side on the true downloaded byte lengths** (never the browser's figure), with an operator-facing sentence that names the limit and the actual total — not a 500, not a silent truncation. **ORDERING IS THE WHOLE CORRECTNESS STORY.** Both routes already send before they write, so every attachment refusal — unreadable draft, over the ceiling, duplicate slot, >10 files — happens **before the send**: 400, nothing sent, nothing written, ticket unmoved. The thread can therefore never show a reply claiming files the member never received. After the send there is nothing left to refuse, so `fileOutboundAttachments()` **never throws and never fails the response** (the email is already with the member; a 500 there would have someone resend it). **Quota goes through the one existing path** — `add_email_storage_bytes` (mig 496), reserve → read the post-increment total → `exceedsQuota()` → release on refusal. A sent attachment costs the same 5 GB-per-mailbox budget a received one does. A **full** mailbox does not unsend anything: the file went out and the row records `skipped_reason:'quota'`, so the chip reads "Not stored — mailbox was full", true in every particular. **The object MOVES** draft key → canonical `<location_id>/<message_id>/<index>.<ext>` once the message row exists, which the inbound shim deliberately does not do — justified here because it *consumes the draft* (without it the same reference could be attached to two sends, leaving two rows pointing at one object that a prune of either would destroy) and because its failure branch has a good answer the shim's lacked: keep the draft key on the row, since nothing in this system derives an address from a prefix. **A sent attachment is indistinguishable from a received one everywhere downstream** — same table, same columns, same `stored XOR skipped` CHECK — so the thread chip, the preview allow-list, the download route, the prune and the counter recalc all picked it up with **zero changes**. UI: one `AttachmentPicker` mounted by both composers (upload starts the moment a file is chosen, so the waiting happens while they type; Send is honestly disabled until everything lands; × discards the object as well as the chip via `POST …/discard`, which can only ever reach the caller's own drafts). An internal note cannot carry files — the picker is hidden in note mode, switching to it with files attached says so and blocks rather than silently dropping them, and the route refuses the combination. **Mobile is OUT, stated:** `mobile/app/email/[ticketId].jsx` can already *view* attachments; adding *sending* needs a document/image picker, the RN `fetch(uri)`→`arrayBuffer` workaround (`mobile/lib/upload-bytes.js`) and real device QA, and the two send routes are about to take a recipients (To/Cc/Bcc) change — the server contract is mobile-ready and unchanged when it lands. Tests +101 (21 pure rules incl. the headroom arithmetic against the real encoder, 24 server IO, 21 upload-sign, 7 discard, 24 across the two route suites, 4 at the wire in `email-inbox-send.test.js`). 11,077 → 11,178 green; all eight CI checks + `next build` clean. **Not verified against real Postmark or a real browser** — no live send with a file, no device QA. |
| 489 | EMAIL-ATTACH-RACE.1 — an inbound photo appears without a page reload | **No migration.** An operator got a member's email with a photo and the thread showed the message with NO attachment; a manual browser reload showed it correctly (live, 2026-08-07). The brief diagnosed a realtime race — **the mechanism was different, and the difference decided the fix.** `email_inbox_messages` and `email_tickets` ARE in the `supabase_realtime` publication (migs 394/482) and `email_ticket_attachments` is not, all as described — but **nothing on this surface subscribes to any of them.** `TicketInbox.jsx` says so in a comment: realtime is deliberately unwired here because mig 485's RESTRICTIVE-`FOR ALL` history means "a listener that silently never fires is a real failure mode", so the QUEUE polls at 60s + on window focus. The real defect is read-side: **the open THREAD was fetched exactly once per selection and never again** (mobile was worse — one load on mount, no poll, no focus refresh at all). The webhook's `create` path inserts the `email_tickets` row FIRST (queue-visible immediately), then the message, then `storeInboundAttachments()` — so a queue poll inside that window surfaces the ticket, the operator clicks, and `loadThread` makes a correct read of an incomplete moment. Nothing was wrong with that read; the bug is that it was the LAST one. **Fix: the open thread re-reads itself**, at a cadence derived from the thread (`threadRefreshMs`) — 5s while its newest message is under 2 minutes old and rows may still be arriving, the queue's 60s otherwise, plus window focus on web. **Chosen over "touch the message row + subscribe" and "publish `email_ticket_attachments` + subscribe" for one reason: both put the fix behind a notification step that can fail**, and if it fails the operator is back to a frozen thread with no reload-free recovery. A self-reading thread has no such step, so a slow upload, a Postmark retry or a Storage blip is picked up by the next read. (Also: `email_inbox_messages` has **no `updated_at`**, so option 1 needed DDL too; option 2's publication change is DDL I must not apply, which would ship the fix inert. Attachments-before-message is refused by the FK and inverts the rule that filing the mail outranks keeping the file.) The **skipped** case (`rehost_failed`/`quota`/`too_many`) is written in the same loop and was equally invisible — same fix, and it matters more there because that row exists precisely to explain itself. **Two consequential side-effects handled:** the thread's auto-scroll now keys on `threadSignature()` (message set, not contents) so a poll cannot drag an operator back to the bottom mid-read, and an attachment landing on a message already on screen moves nothing; and the re-read is `quiet` — it paints no spinner and **no error**, because a blip on a background read must never replace correspondence someone is reading with a failure message. **Ticket list: no change needed** (already polls + refreshes on focus; on the `append` path the ticket bump runs after the attachments anyway). Mobile got the same cadence as a deliberate re-statement (`mobile/lib/email-tickets.js` — mobile cannot import `src/lib`), with a test asserting the constants have not drifted from web. **Not verified live:** that the photo actually appears within the settle window against real Postmark + Storage timings — the tests pin the schedule, not the delivery. |
| 488 | EMAIL-CC.1 — multiple recipients, Cc and Bcc on email tickets, end to end | **Mig 499 APPLIED 2026-08-07.** Cc/Bcc were in the original ticketing spec and the SCHEMA SHIPPED WITHOUT THE WIRING: `email_inbox_messages.cc_emails` / `bcc_emails` landed with mig 482 (`text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'`) and nothing ever wrote or read them — the same inert-column shape the attachment pipeline had. Confirmed against the live schema before building; the brief's guess that inbound Cc needed a new column was **wrong** (it already had one). The only real gap was the To side: `to_email` is a single `text`, so mig 499 adds **`to_emails text[]` BESIDE it** (not instead of — `to_email` stays the PRIMARY recipient, which is what `email_sends` logs and what every pre-499 reader understands) plus a backfill so no reader has to special-case old rows. **REPLY vs REPLY-ALL IS DERIVED, NOT CHOSEN** (Richard, 2026-08-07). Reply = one person; Reply All = everybody on the thread; and when a thread has more than one participant **plain Reply is not offered at all**, because two buttons is precisely the affordance that lets someone silently drop a participant. They are ONE code path: `threadParticipants()` of the LATEST non-note message (its From + To + Cc, minus our own addresses), and whether that returns one person or four is what makes it a reply or a reply-all. The button says which — *"Reply All (4 people)"*. Only the latest message counts (mail clients follow the latest message; resurrecting someone a member deliberately dropped would re-copy them over the member's head). Participants are ALWAYS included server-side — `to`/`cc`/`bcc` in the body only ADD — so narrowing a conversation means starting a new email, a deliberate act with its own button. **BCC, BOTH DIRECTIONS.** Outbound: `toPostmarkFields()` is the single site where a resolved set becomes wire values, and bcc reaches Postmark's own `Bcc` field and nothing else — never a header, never folded into To/Cc (Postmark strips the Bcc header from delivered mail; verified against their docs, and their 2024 SMTP header change says API sending was never affected). Inbound-to-us: `bcc_emails` is **never an input to a later send** — `threadParticipants()` does not name the column, and the reply route does not even SELECT it, so a reply, a reply-all or the forward that reuses this model all reach exactly the people they would have reached had the Bcc never been typed. Mig 482 created `email_ticket_attachments` and the private `email-attachments` bucket and mig 483 made its RLS work, but both shipped **inert**: the table had zero rows and nothing in the codebase wrote it — the Postmark inbound webhook never looked at the `Attachments` array at all, so **every file a member has ever sent was discarded on arrival, silently**. Metering storage without storing anything would have metered nothing, so both halves land together. **Storage.** `storeInboundAttachments()` (`src/lib/email-attachments-server.js`) runs AFTER the message insert in `postmark-inbound/[token]`, and it is **subordinate to filing the message** — it never throws, answers nothing the route branches on, and records a row with a `skipped_reason` for anything it cannot keep, so an oversized file, a full mailbox or a Storage outage all still leave the member's email filed and readable. Mig 482's `email_attach_stored_xor_skipped` XOR is honoured in both directions. **Hostile filenames are DATA.** `Name` arrives from an unauthenticated stranger; the object key is `<location_id>/<message_id>/<index>.<ext>` — every component ours, ids validated against a bare-path-segment regex, extension derived from the sanitised MIME essence and stripped to `[a-z0-9]{1,8}`. `safeAttachmentFilename()` keeps the original for **display only**, stripping control chars (**Postgres text cannot hold a NUL at all — left in, the insert fails and takes the record with it**), bidi overrides (the `report<U+202E>gnp.exe` spoof), path separators, and **lone surrogates**, then truncating by CODE POINT so the cut can never manufacture one. **Byte length is the decoded buffer's** — never `Content.length`, never the sender's `ContentLength`. **Quota, per mailbox (Richard).** New `email_storage_usage` + `add_email_storage_bytes()` RPC on the mig 314 atomic-counter pattern; the RPC returns the total AFTER its own increment and the writer **reserves then checks then rolls back on refusal**, so two attachments landing together cannot both be told there is room (check-then-reserve is the lost-update race the counter exists to remove). **Divergence from the spec, deliberate:** the spec keys the table `mailbox_id PRIMARY KEY`, which has no answer for `email_tickets.mailbox_id` being ON DELETE SET NULL — those bytes would escape accounting or NOT-NULL-crash the write. Key is `(location_id, mailbox_id)` `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG17), NULL = the location's **unfiled** bucket, same 5 GB ceiling, visible to exactly the people who can see unfiled tickets, prunable. Also deliberate: `bytes_used` counts **stored attachment bytes only**, not body lengths as the spec wanted — the same spec forbids ever pruning bodies, and metering what no release valve can reclaim turns a full mailbox into a permanently full one. **Idempotency.** The webhook releases its dedupe claim on any 5xx (EMAIL-DEDUPE-RELEASE.1) precisely so Postmark's retry re-processes, which makes double processing **designed**, not hypothetical. `attachment_index` is the file's position in Postmark's own array — identical on every retry — under `UNIQUE (message_id, attachment_index)`; a pre-check skips the work, a 23505 is the race-safe backstop, and both **release the reservation**. The 23505 path leaves the uploaded object alone on purpose: the key is deterministic, so it is byte-identical to what the winning row points at. Pinned by a test that posts the same payload twice and asserts the counter reads one file's worth. **Serving.** `GET /api/email/tickets/{id}/attachments/{attachmentId}` mints a 5-minute signed URL, reusing `loadTicketForUser` (location + mailbox gate) plus **one extra check that the attachment belongs to THIS ticket** — without that pairing check any ticket a coach can open would unlock any attachment id in the estate. 404 never 403 throughout; `storage_path` is never returned. Attachments now ride the ticket GET payload (`stored` + `skipped_reason`, never the path) and render in `TicketThread`; a failed attachment query reports `attachments_unavailable` rather than rendering as "no files" (the EMAIL-TICKET.6 silent-wrong-answer shape). **Surfacing + the way down.** `GET/POST /api/locations/{id}/email/storage` and a Storage card on the existing Email tab: per-account bar with 80/95/100% levels, the unfiled bucket when it exists, a **Free up space** action (attachments older than a year on **solved/closed tickets only** — a ticket someone is still working is never touched) and a **Recalculate** repair. Pruning **decrements the counter**: rows are marked first (`storage_path` NULL + new `skipped_reason` `'pruned'`, so staff still see the file existed and can ask for a resend), the UPDATE filters on `storage_path IS NOT NULL` and decrements by what it *actually changed* so two concurrent prunes cannot double-count, and a failed object removal still decrements and shouts (rows and counter agreeing is what keeps the mailbox usable; a leaked object is a cost line). Gate is `guardMailboxAdmin` — master/owner-at-location, NOT `email_inbox`, since a manager holds that key and prune destroys correspondence. **Body-size finding, flagged not fixed:** nothing in the route, `next.config.mjs` or `vercel.json` caps the request body (App Router has no `bodyParser.sizeLimit`), but **Vercel rejects a Node-function body over ~4.5 MB with a 413 before the handler runs** — and Postmark base64-inlines attachments (~4/3), so the practical inbound ceiling is ~3.3 MB of attachment bytes per email, far under Postmark's 25 MB. A larger mail never reaches the `too_large` branch: Postmark sees a 413 and the message is not filed. Pre-existing for every inbound email (bodies too), documented in the route header; the fix is Postmark's strip-attachments-and-fetch-by-URL mode, not code here. **Tests:** +99 (34 lib IO incl. the double-process proof and every failure mode, 31 pure filename/path/quota incl. the NUL / bidi / lone-surrogate / traversal cases, 10 serving-route incl. the cross-ticket IDOR, 18 operator-route, 6 webhook). The shared ticket test double now models the unique index, the counter RPC and the bucket for real — a stubbed RPC would make every quota assertion pass with the check deleted. Full CI mirror + `next build` green. **Not verified end-to-end against real Postmark or real Storage; no device QA.** |

| 467 | ZOOMSYNC.3 — repaired 30 of the 46 bare-digit phone numbers ZOOMSYNC.2 rejects | **30 rows repaired live 2026-08-06 (22 `+1`, 7 `+44`, 1 `+30`); 16 left bare on purpose.** ZOOMSYNC.2 (#1235) stopped `normaliseForZoom()` fabricating a country code out of a bare number's leading digits (`!hasPlus && digits.length < 11`), so the 46 non-ClassPass rows storing a phone as 8 or 10 bare digits (37 ten-digit, 9 eight-digit; measured 2026-08-06) are now simply absent from the Zoom caller-ID directory rather than published wrong. That fixed the sync, not the data. New `src/lib/zoom/infer-bare-phone.js` + `scripts/audit-bare-phones.mjs` classify each row into three tiers so the repair is evidence-led rather than guessed. **The tiering is the whole point:** `derived` means a known-good E.164 already on the contact — `contacts.wa_phone`, or a `whatsapp_conversations` thread — *ends with* the stored bare digits, so the stored value is a truncation of a number we already hold and the country code is **read off, not inferred**; the repair writes that held number verbatim rather than assembling a prefix, so it cannot fabricate a code even when the remainder is an odd length. This is the same suffix-match evidence LEADCAP.2 (#462) used to justify `IE_MOBILE_BARE` for the 431 nine-digit Irish rows, so it is a pattern already trusted in this repo, not a new leap. `corroborated` needs the digit shape to map to exactly one country **and** an independent non-phone signal (email ccTLD) to agree — a proposal for review, never an instruction. **Two rules the live data disproved before anything was written:** (a) currency was a signal (`EUR`→`+353`) — it reflects the *merchant*, not the member, since UN1T bills every member in EUR from Dublin, so it was both wrong reasoning and useless (only 2 of the 46 have any invoice, both EUR); removed. (b) There was no UK-mobile hypothesis, and **7 of the 37 ten-digit rows are UK mobiles that lost their trunk zero** (`07xxx xxxxxx` bare = `7[1-9]`+8), so "bare 10 digits ≈ North American" was wrong for a fifth of the population. Two of those seven (`7300093740`, `7400183722`) sit on assigned NANP area codes (IL 730, OH 740) and would have been published as US numbers with full confidence — the exact wrong-number harm ZOOMSYNC.2 exists to prevent. What separates them is the **central-office code**, which in NANP can never begin 0 or 1; both carry one (`…009…`, `…018…`), so they resolve to a clean UK read. Checking only the area code would have stranded two repairable numbers in `ambiguous` *and* mislabelled them had the exchange been valid. Everything else is `ambiguous` and is **left alone by design**: a bare 10-digit number is probably North American but could be a mistyped Irish one, and guessing wrong writes a stranger's number against a real member's name, which is the exact harm ZOOMSYNC.2 closed. **Why an assigned-area-code list rather than the `[2-9]\d\d` structural rule:** the Greek row that surfaced this, `6978291516`, is structurally a valid NANP area code (`697`) and a bare structural test would have proposed `+16978291516` with a straight face; `697` is unassigned, so membership in the list is what refuses the NANP reading and leaves the Greek one (+30, mobiles are `69X` + 7). A missing code only demotes a row to `ambiguous`, which is the safe direction to be wrong in. Script is **read-only by default**; `--apply` writes *only* the `derived` tier, and any other row must be named by id (`--apply --ids=…`), which is what stops it becoming the bulk `UPDATE … SET phone = '+1' \|\| phone` that would reintroduce the original defect. Every write is re-checked through `normaliseForZoom()` first, so a repair the sync would reject again is refused. 31 co-located tests, including both directions of an agreement check against the live normaliser (in-scope ⇒ rejected, out-of-scope ⇒ accepted) so the triage cannot drift off the population it targets. **The corroborating context the task assumed simply does not exist for this population:** all 46 have **zero bookings, zero WhatsApp threads and zero contact events**, `last_attended` is `never` for every one, and 44 of 46 were created on 2026-05-12 in a single bulk import. So the `derived` tier — the one that reads a country code off a number we already hold — matched **nothing**, because not one of the 46 has a `wa_phone` or a WhatsApp conversation. Digit shape was the only evidence available, which is defensible here for one specific reason: a bare 10-digit number beginning 2–9 **cannot be Irish** (Irish mobiles are 9 bare digits, landlines 8), so the "it might be a mistyped Irish number" worry that motivated leaving these alone does not apply to the ten-digit bucket. Applied: 22 `+1`, 7 `+44`, 1 `+30` — every value re-checked through `normaliseForZoom()` before the write (30/30 round-trip). **16 deliberately left bare:** 4 are Irish mobile prefixes (`83/85/86/89`) one digit **short** of a complete number — truncation damage, and a lost digit is unrecoverable, not a missing country code; 2 are the same number (`3174278753`) stored against two different people, which is a data bug to resolve before either is published; 1 is a Glofox internal record (`@glofox.com`) that self-excluded on an invalid NANP exchange and should never reach a shared directory; the remaining 9 have no confident reading. Those 16 stay invisible to Zoom via the ZOOMSYNC.2 reject, which is the correct outcome — chase them by asking the member, not by guessing. Repairs need no backfill: the nightly `/api/cron/zoom-contact-sync` reconcile recomputes desired state from `contacts`. **Reconciles with the count in 466:** the first real run published **6,078** entries with all 46 of these excluded, so the next run adds the 30 repaired here (≈6,108) — a jump in `creates` on an otherwise steady directory is expected once, and is this task, not a boundary regression. Out of scope and still open: ~219 non-ClassPass contacts with no phone at all and ~32 with genuinely malformed values (curly quotes, a stray `#`, an email in the phone field). |

| 461 | RLS-RESTRICTIVE.1 — a restrictive `FOR ALL` deny-writes policy was also denying SELECT on 16 tables, silently killing realtime | Postgres evaluates RLS as (OR of permissive) AND (AND of restrictive), and `FOR ALL` includes SELECT — so `AS RESTRICTIVE FOR ALL TO authenticated, anon USING (false)` folded each table's permissive SELECT policy away entirely (`EXPLAIN` shows `One-Time Filter: false`). Supabase realtime authorises every `postgres_changes` row through the subscriber's SELECT policy, so the four affected tables in the publication (`email_conversations`/`email_inbox_messages` mig 394, `instagram_conversations`/`instagram_messages` mig 231+256) delivered **nothing, ever** — dead listeners in `EmailInbox.jsx` (both), `IGInbox.jsx` (both) and `UnifiedInbox.jsx` (4 of its 7 tables), masked for months by the 60s poll beneath them. WAInbox + templates unaffected (WA tables never got a restrictive policy). **Mig 485** splits the restrictive on all 16 tables into per-command `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` restrictives `TO authenticated`, keeping a `FOR ALL TO anon` backstop — the shape diverges from mig 483 (which used `TO authenticated, anon`) because 6 of the 16 have a `TO public` SELECT policy, where copying 483 verbatim would newly subject anon to it. Write denial is redundant today (no permissive write policy on any of the 16; verified) but retained as the backstop against a future careless permissive write policy. **Not touched, deliberately:** 8 tables with no permissive SELECT at all (mig 168's advisor-lint cleanup, `device_tokens`, `champ_push_tokens`, `push_event_sends` — nothing to unblock, splitting would only remove a backstop), `push_reminder_sends` (restrictive is `TO anon` only, so authenticated SELECT always worked — it is the correct pattern), and `storage.objects` (mig 403's restrictive is conditional, not `USING (false)`; denying SELECT on private buckets is its entire purpose). Enumerated by replaying every migration in order for net policy state, not grepping `CREATE POLICY`. New `check:rls-restrictive` CI gate fails on the pattern — verified failing on the pre-fix tree (exactly 16) and passing after. **APPLIED** 2026-08-06 (`20260806000336`). Verified live: `pg_policies` confirmed the same 16 tables the migration-replay found (no dashboard drift); pre-fix `EXPLAIN` as `authenticated` gave `One-Time Filter: false` on all 7 sampled tables while the controls `contacts` (no restrictive) and `email_tickets` (fixed by 483) planned normally; post-fix all 16 READ as `authenticated` and all 16 stay DENIED as `anon`. Authorising as a real staff user the way realtime does (`request.jwt.claims` + `SET ROLE authenticated`), `email_conversations` went 0 → 1 row visible, while UPDATE affected 0 rows, INSERT raised 42501 and DELETE affected 0 — reads restored, writes still denied. `wallets` correctly still returns 0 rows for a non-master user, so the policies' own logic is intact rather than blanket-opened. The defect predicate now matches 0 tables estate-wide. Advisors: security has no ERROR and names none of the 16; performance is 207 lints, all INFO (`unused_index` / `unindexed_foreign_keys`), none policy-related, and notably no `multiple_permissive_policies`. **Not** verified: a browser watching a message land — that needs an `authenticated` websocket JWT, which would mean minting a session against a real staff account or creating a test user in production auth. The publication membership and the per-row RLS decision (the two things 485 changed) are both confirmed live; the transport leg is exercised continuously by the WhatsApp tables in the same publication. |
| 460 | CSP-AUDIT.1 — `frame-ancestors *` investigated: already correctly scoped, no code change | Raised as a clickjacking concern (any origin can iframe the authenticated CRM) off the email-ticketing spec's "not in scope, but noticed" note. **The premise was wrong and nothing needed fixing.** `next.config.js` ships `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` on `/(.*)` and grants `frame-ancestors *` to exactly two subtrees — `/embed/:path*` and `/book/:path*` — deliberately, in AUDIT-JUN10.2 (#409), after a path-to-regexp negative-lookahead exclusion was tried and found to mis-match (`/bookings` lost the header). Confirmed **against production**, not just the config: `/login`, `/tv/*`, `/host`, `/ccf` all return SAMEORIGIN with no CSP; only `/embed/*` + `/book/*` carry the override. Every surface named as a possible reason for a broad setting was checked and needs no framing — the TV displays are fullscreen kiosk/cast surfaces, and the events page's Instagram strip is the app *embedding* IG (outbound `frame-src`), the opposite direction to `frame-ancestors`. The two genuinely-embedded surfaces are precisely the two exempted, and both iframe-code generators agree (`EventActions.jsx` emits `/book/<slug>`, `LandingPageSettingsForm.jsx` emits `/embed/event/<slug>`). `*` kept over an origin allowlist on purpose: both are unauthenticated public signup/booking forms carrying no session and no CRM data, and paste-anywhere is the product requirement. **What actually shipped is the doc fix**, because three separate places had drifted into stating the header was global and that is what generated the false alarm: the `/embed/event/[slug]` page comment still claimed "no X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors are set app-wide" (false since June — the route is framable by *exemption*, and anyone deleting it would break every third-party embed silently), the IG-strip spec omitted the path scoping, and the email-ticketing spec's follow-up note is now closed as resolved. `next.config.js` gains a comment at the `frameable` const saying it is not a global policy. **Separately assessed, no action taken:** the app still has no `default-src`/`script-src` anywhere. The blocker is architectural — `headers()` is static and cannot emit a per-request nonce, so a nonce-based CSP has to live in `src/proxy.js`, not here; there is an inline `<script>` on every public landing page (`reveal-arm.js`) plus Next's own hydration scripts, and no nonce infrastructure exists. A future policy would also need `editor.unlayer.com` (script + its own iframe), `unpkg.com` (`/api-docs`), and `frame-src` for youtube/instagram. Good news for email-ticketing: React's raw-HTML escape hatch is used **nowhere** in `src/`, and because that feature renders via `srcdoc` — which *inherits* the parent's CSP — a global policy would cover the email document for free if it ever lands (noted in the spec). |

Fixing the badge that lied only helps someone who goes and looks, and for 17 days nobody did — so this is the part that shouts. The register form now asks for the hostname so bridges are linked at birth rather than the column lying dormant — NULL remains legitimate and degrades to reachability-only, exactly like a kiosk. Push is sent **categoryless** on purpose (the `resolvePermission` fail-closed trap that bit `app_update` and `test`), plus email to masters as the durable record; both are best-effort so one Postmark hiccup can't stop the fleet being checked. Two deliberate non-alerts: a Tailscale API failure is not a fleet outage (it would page all six at once), and zero tagged devices means a mis-scoped OAuth client, not six destroyed Pis. **Ships dark** — with `TAILSCALE_OAUTH_*` unset the route no-ops and still stamps its heartbeat, so merging changes nothing until it's configured; the go-live step that matters is watching one 04:00 cycle produce no alerts. Known limit, documented in the spec: a kiosk that is powered and on the tailnet but showing a black screen (the lightdm crash-loop of 2026-08-02) still reads `ok` — catching that needs device-side reporting and is the strongest argument for a future kiosk heartbeat. | 452 | BRIDGE-STATUS.1 — the admin bridges badge read ONLINE for a bridge dead 17 days | PR #1193. Found 2026-08-02 while provisioning the new Stillorgan Pi 5: `ble_bridges.last_seen_at` was 2026-07-16, no `hr_samples` since, and **1,186 heart-rate sessions created with zero samples** across the outage — yet `/admin/bridges` showed a green ONLINE chip with "Last seen 15 days ago" rendered directly beside it, so nobody noticed for over two weeks. Root cause: `status` only ever moves one way. `/api/bridge/heartbeat` writes `status: 'online'` on every beat and **nothing writes it back** — a Pi that loses power cannot send a final 'offline'. This was already a known trap elsewhere in the codebase: both `src/lib/live-board.js` and `src/lib/bridge-samples.js` carry comments saying the column "can lie" and deliberately key the TV connection dot off `last_seen_at` freshness instead. The admin surface was simply the one place still rendering the raw column. Fix reuses that existing machinery rather than inventing a threshold: new pure `deriveBridgeStatus(bridge, nowMs)` in `bridge-samples.js` sits on `isBridgeOnline`/`BRIDGE_ONLINE_WINDOW_MS` (60s = two missed 30s heartbeats), and `GET /api/admin/bridges` maps it over the rows so the badge and the live board cannot disagree. Freshness outranks the column in ONE direction only — a bridge still heartbeating and self-reporting `'error'` keeps 'error', because that state is meaningful and set by the bridge itself; a *stale* error becomes offline. Also fixes the "N straps visible" line, which was gated on `status === 'online'` and so claimed straps for a dead bridge. **No migration** — the column is left alone as the bridge's own self-report; this is a display-derivation change. Known limit: `BridgesAdmin` fetches once on mount and does not poll, so a page left open goes stale — but the badge and the "last seen" text freeze together, so they stay consistent. |

Geofence attendance (mig 463) only fires on a recent build WITH background location granted, and the CRM knew neither — a silent no-fire was undiagnosable. Now: one pure lib (`src/lib/staff-devices.js`, injected clock, no `Date.now()` inside) owns every verdict, and three surfaces consume it so they can't disagree — the EXISTING `/settings/notifications/health` page (extended, not duplicated: it already loaded every `device_tokens` row), a Device column + `Needs update` filter on `/settings/staff`, and a Devices card on the staff profile. Rules: **newest device wins, not best version** (an old iPad on a newer build must not mask a daily phone that never updated); a device unseen for 30d is stale and may never set the target version (an abandoned beta would otherwise put the fleet permanently "behind"); the target is the highest parseable version among non-stale ACTIVE-staff devices, so it self-updates with no operator setting; `parseVersion` rejects segments >9999 because `app_version` is client-reported and the highest value in the fleet is the bar everyone is judged against. Mobile (JS-only, rides the 2.2.0 OTA lane): `LocationGate`'s foreground `check` maps the two OS permission reads to one value and fires the new `reportDeviceState()` only when it CHANGED (ref), never while impersonating or without a session, fire-and-forget in its own try/catch; `reportDeviceState()` also reports `app_version` WITHOUT the push-permission flow, fixing the gap where anyone who declined notifications looked like they had no app at all. **TRAP (mig 466 columns, and any future column here):** the `device_tokens` upsert conflict target is `expo_push_token`, so an upsert rewrites the whole row and an OMITTED key nulls the stored value — `geofence_permission`/`_at` are spread in only when the client actually sent one, or every register from a pre-2.2.0 build would wipe them. NULL renders as `—`, **never** as "denied": absence of data is not a denial, and conflating them destroys the diagnostic. Nudge: `POST /api/staff-devices/nudge` recomputes who is outdated SERVER-SIDE and intersects with the requested ids (the client sends ids, never verdicts), skips `no_device` (no token by definition), throttles to one per device per 24h on `last_update_nudge_at` — stamped only when a push actually landed, so an Expo outage can't lock the operator out for a day — and reports a push failure in the counts rather than 500ing. It deliberately sends **no `category`**: `sendPush` gates on `notify_<category>` and `resolvePermission`'s last tier is `defaults[role][key] === true`, so an UNREGISTERED key resolves to FALSE — `category: 'app_update'` would have skipped every staffer with a location assignment and reached nobody (the same latent trap sat under `/api/admin/push/test`'s category `'test'` — found here, fixed in 449). Android routing moved to `data.type` → the existing Updates channel. Also fixed in passing: the health page's `StatusPill` amber used `text-amber-200`, invisible on the light surface. Full reference: `docs/staff-devices.md`. |
| 447 | RESET-PKCE.1 — password reset / invite links could never verify (PKCE code verifier deleted by our own sign-out) | Operator-reported 2026-07-31 (staff hit "Reset link could not be verified: this link is missing its verification token"). `/reset-password` and `/host/set-password` both did `signOut({ scope: 'local' })` as a "clean slate" step BEFORE `exchangeCodeForSession(code)`. auth-js `_removeSession()` removes `${storageKey}-code-verifier` along with the session (and runs for ANY scope except `'others'`, even with no session present), so the sign-out destroyed the PKCE verifier the very next line needed — and @supabase/ssr pins `flowType: 'pkce'`, so `?code=` is the only shape those links take. Every reset died with `AuthPKCECodeVerifierMissingError`; re-clicking the by-then-consumed link came back as `#error=access_denied&error_code=otp_expired`, which the page read as "no token present" and mislabelled as a malformed link. Confirmed live: `auth.flow_state` for the reporting user showed `authentication_method='recovery'`, `code_challenge_method='s256'`, `auth_code_issued_at` set — and zero `auth.sessions` rows. Fix: new `src/lib/recovery-link.js` (`parseRecoveryLink` + `establishRecoverySession`, 15 tests) owns the handshake for both pages — establish the session FIRST, sign out only on the failure paths. The 2026-05-13 wrong-account guard is preserved differently: a successful exchange/setSession/verifyOtp overwrites storage with the LINK's user, `getUser()` must confirm that same id before the form unlocks, and `handleReset` re-checks the live session id against it at the moment of the write. GoTrue error bounces now say "expired or already been used", and a cross-browser open (email app's in-app browser vs the browser that requested the link — PKCE binds the two) says so instead of leaking the SDK string. |

| 420 | CONTRACTS-PDF.1 — signed PDF artifact (generate, store, attach, download) | Closes the "PDF generation is deliberately deferred" stub in `src/app/api/contracts/[id]/sign/route.js`. **Library:** `@react-pdf/renderer` ^4.5.1 added to the ROOT `package.json` (52 transitive packages, ~3MB, pure JS + a wasm yoga layout engine — no headless browser, no native `.node` binary, nothing to add to the serverless bundle beyond JS; the PDF standard-14 Times faces are built in so there is no font file to ship either). Verified rendering server-side in plain Node with no DOM and under vitest's node environment. **New `src/lib/contract-pdf.js`:** `parseContractBlocks(markdown)` is a pure function splitting the frozen `body_rendered` into `{type:'heading',level,text}` / `{type:'list',items}` / `{type:'hr'}` / `{type:'paragraph',runs}`, with `**bold**` becoming `[{text,bold}]` runs via the also-exported `parseInlineRuns`. react-markdown (what `ContractBody.jsx` uses for the web view) could not be reused: it emits DOM elements react-pdf cannot render. GOVERNING RULE, stated in the file header: a legal document must never silently lose content, so every unrecognised construct (blockquotes, tables, links, raw HTML) renders as its literal source characters rather than being dropped — ugly beats missing. Two documented deviations from a strict `#`/`##`/`###` reading: `####`+ clamps to level 3 (ContractBody renders h4-h6 as real headings on the web, so a literal `#### x` in the PDF would diverge from the document the recipient signed, and clamping loses nothing), and an ordered-list line flushes the running paragraph so numbered clauses do not glue into one run-on block (still a `paragraph`, still carrying its literal `1. ` marker). `renderContractPdf({...})` maps those blocks onto react-pdf primitives via `React.createElement` (NOT JSX — a `.js` file under `src/lib` would hit vitest's esbuild `js` loader, which does not parse JSX) and returns a Buffer: A4, Times, 56pt margins, a fixed company-name/template-name header, a fixed `Page X of Y` footer, and a dual signature block matching the web layout (two 50% columns, "For \<companyName\>" / "Employee / Contractor", italic typed names, `Europe/Dublin` timestamps via the existing `formatFullDateTimeInTZ`, IP under the recipient). **Sign route:** after the status flip + detail fetch and before the emails, the whole PDF step (branding via `getLocationBranding` → render → `db.storage.from('contracts').upload('<id>/signed.pdf', buf, {contentType, upsert:true})` → awaited `signed_pdf_path` update) sits in one try/catch that pushes onto the route's existing `warnings` array. The sign itself can never fail on a PDF error — the DB row is the legal record and failing here would tell a recipient their signature did not go through when the row is already committed; the stale "deliberately deferred" comment was replaced with that reasoning. The buffer deliberately survives a STORAGE failure so the emails can still carry the attachment even when `/pdf` has nothing to serve yet. **Email:** `sendEmail` in `src/lib/postmark.js` gained a purely additive optional `attachments` passthrough (Postmark's own `[{Name, Content: base64, ContentType}]` shape; the `Attachments` key is only added when non-empty, so every existing caller's payload is byte-identical). `sendContractSignedEmails` gained an optional `pdfBuffer` — when present both the recipient and issuer emails attach `signed-contract.pdf`; over an 8MB raw ceiling (Postmark's cap is 10MB for the whole message and base64 inflates ~33%) the attachment is skipped and `results.warning` is set, which the sign route folds into its warnings, rather than losing the notification. **Download:** new `GET /api/contracts/[id]/pdf` mints a 60-second Supabase Storage signed URL and 302s to it — the `contracts` bucket (mig 106) stays private and no public URL is ever produced. Authorization mirrors `GET /api/contracts/[id]` exactly (recipient / master / org-owner, 404-not-403 so ids stay non-enumerable, plus the same draft-is-404-for-a-recipient-only-caller clause kept purely so the two gates cannot drift); `signed_pdf_path` null is also a 404. Registered in `src/lib/openapi.js` beside the other Contracts entries. Both `/admin/contracts/[id]` and `/account/contracts/[id]` render a "Download PDF" `print:hidden` link-button, styled like `ContractPrintButton`, only when `c.signed_pdf_path` is set (plain `<a>`, not `<Link>` — the 302 to Storage is a real navigation). **Tests:** 36 in `src/lib/contract-pdf.test.js` (headings incl. the `####` clamp and the `#tag` non-heading, list grouping/regrouping/interruption, hr forms incl. rejecting `--`, soft-wrap joining, CRLF, ordered-list splitting, bold runs incl. an unterminated `**` staying literal, empty/whitespace/non-string input, and a never-lose-a-line assertion over a realistic contract) plus two renderer smoke tests that assert a real non-empty `%PDF-` Buffer — the renderer runs fine under vitest, so nothing needed skipping; the PDF binary is deliberately NOT snapshotted (react-pdf embeds a creation timestamp). 10 route tests for the pdf GET (401, 404 foreign-staff + foreign-org-owner with `createSignedUrl` never called, 404 no-pdf-yet, 404 recipient-draft, 302 for recipient/org-owner/master, 500 on a failed mint with no Location header) and 4 email tests (attaches to both, absent when no buffer, oversized skip + warning, zero-length ignored). No migration (mig 106 already created the bucket and the `signed_pdf_path` column, both unused until now). Full local CI mirror green; `npm run build` left to CI. Not verified end to end against real Storage/Postmark. |

| 418 | CONTRACTS-VARS.2 — per-variable defaults + location auto-fill vocabulary | Two additions to the contracts engine, both no-migration (`variables_schema` is JSONB). **Per-variable defaults:** `contractVariableDefSchema` gains optional `default` (string, omitted rather than persisted empty). `ContractTemplateForm.jsx`'s custom-variable row gained a "default" input (date type renders a date input, matching the wizard's own input rendering; grid re-spanned key/label/type/default/required/remove as 2/3/2/2/2/1 across 12). `ContractIssueWizard.jsx` seeds `vars` from a template's declared defaults whenever the SELECTED TEMPLATE actually changes (a `useEffect` keyed on the memoized `template` object, not on every render) — precedence is default < re-issue prefill < issuer typing: the B2 prefill's custom variables are stashed in a ref (`pendingPrefillVarsRef`) rather than set directly, since the two mount-time fetches (staff+templates vs. the prefill contract) resolve in either order and only the ref survives to whichever one resolves `template` last; issuer typing wins simply because nothing re-runs the effect until `templateId` changes again. | 398 | Mia — auto-hand-off after repeated identity-verification failure | After **N (default 2)** consecutive failed `verify_identity` attempts in a conversation, Mia stops re-asking and hands off to a human instead of looping the email+surname quiz (Richard hit a 3× loop). **Mig 433** (applied) adds `agent_verify_attempts smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` to `whatsapp_conversations` + `instagram_conversations`. Counting lives in pure `core.js` helpers (`resolveVerifyFailHandoff` — settings `handoff_after_verify_failures`, 0 disables; `shouldHandoffAfterVerifyFail`; `nextVerifyAttempts`); `auto-reply.js` seeds the counter from the conversation, updates it per `verify_identity` result in the tool loop (reset on success, +1 on failure), and after the loop — if the threshold is met — calls the existing `handoff()` (reason `verify_failed`; standard holding message + manager page + SLA re-alert), discarding the model's retry text. Counter resets on success, on the forced handoff, and on agent re-arm. Only the email-quiz path is affected (phone-auto-verified senders never call `verify_identity`); WhatsApp + Instagram via the shared loop. No settings-UI field in v1 (tunable via the settings blob). | 397 | Mia — fix unwinnable identity quiz when a WhatsApp number has duplicate contacts | A member texting from a number with several contact rows could be permanently unable to verify: `verify_identity`'s linked path (`src/lib/agent/account-tools.js`) matched the provided email against **only the thread's bound `contact_id`**. When the conversation was pinned to a duplicate whose email differed from the member's (e.g. a `test@` dupe with no Glofox membership sitting on the same number as the real `member` row), the customer's correct membership email could never match → "I can't match those details to an account", no email they could truthfully give would work. Now the linked path builds a candidate **pool of every contact sharing the sender's WhatsApp/phone number at the location** (new IO helper `contactsForSender`, mirroring `core.resolveAutoVerify`'s phone match) and verifies if the email matches **any** of them (new pure helper `pickVerifiedContact`; single-contact pools behave exactly as before, so it's a strict, safe broadening — the number is still the second factor, the customer can only type their own email). Stamps the matched contact; auto-reply still resolves it to the person-group primary for the acting account. Unlinked (Instagram / unknown number) path unchanged — still email + surname. Root-caused from Richard's own thread (number `353…7675` had 4 Richard contacts, 3 person-linked + 1 stray `test@` dupe the thread was bound to; the stray was also person-linked as an immediate data fix). Tests: 8 new (pool matching across a sibling dupe, case-insensitivity, no-match, single-contact parity, unlinked email+surname, nameHint; executor stamps the MEMBER not the bound dupe, and still refuses a foreign email). Full CI mirror green. |

| 397 | Repset: plan assignment — pin a tier/add-on to a tenant location (the billing on-switch) | **The missing keystone that makes the already-built billing/wallet/enforcement machinery operable.** Billing is PER-LOCATION: "allocate a plan to a tenant" = pin a plan VERSION to one of the tenant's LOCATIONS via a `location_plans` row (mig 413). Nothing wrote `location_plans` before — every location was unpinned, so `getLocationPlan()` returned null and wallets/enforcement/monthly-reset/meters/billing-page/MRR all sat dormant. Pinning an ACTIVE TIER is the on-switch: `getLocationPlan()` starts returning non-null → the whole billing machine engages **for that location only**. **Write route `POST /api/admin/tenants/[orgId]/plans`** (master-only, mirroring the sibling `/api/admin/tenants` routes' `getCurrentUser`→`profileRole==='master'`→401/403 guard). Body `{ location_id, plan_id|plan_slug, plan_version_id?, kind }`; `plan_version_id` defaults to the plan's CURRENT active version (`getActivePlanVersion`, explicit grandfathering by passing a specific version). Validates: location belongs to `orgId` (**cross-org / unknown → 404 not 403**, IDOR rule); plan exists, is `active`, and its `kind` matches the body; an explicit version belongs to the plan. **THE ONE-ACTIVE-TIER INVARIANT (load-bearing, enforced SERVER-SIDE):** assigning a tier calls `deactivateActiveTierPins()` — a single guarded `UPDATE location_plans SET active=false WHERE location_id=… AND active=true AND plan_version_id IN (<tier version ids>)` — **BEFORE** activating the new tier (deactivate-first ordering), so the only reachable states are one active tier (success) or zero (interrupted → dormant, which `getLocationPlan` treats as unpinned); two active tiers is never reachable through this route. Add-ons are additive (multiple allowed, tier untouched) and idempotent (re-assigning the same add-on keeps exactly one active row). **Unassign `DELETE /api/admin/tenants/[orgId]/plans`** `{ location_id, plan_version_id }` → deactivates that pin; unpinning the tier returns the location to DORMANT (`getLocationPlan` null, billing off), unpinning an add-on just drops it; unknown pin / cross-org → 404. Both registered in `openapi.js`. **UI on the tenant drill-in** (`/admin/tenants/[orgId]`, `TenantDetailView.jsx`): each location shows its pin state ("No plan — dormant" vs active tier + version + price + "Billing active"), an **Assign/Change plan** modal (pick a tier from the active catalogue, version defaulted to current with price shown, consequence copy "activates billing, wallet and usage enforcement for this location"), **add-on toggles** (e.g. custom_email_domain), and a **Set dormant** action ("returns it to dormant — no billing"); every change `router.refresh()`es so pin/MRR/health re-grade immediately. `getTenantDetail` now also returns the assignable `catalogue` (active plans + their current version, via the new pure `buildPlanCatalogue`) and each location's `plan.planVersionId` + active add-on ids. **No migration** — `location_plans` (mig 413) already exists; this only adds the first WRITE path (wallet/enforcement/cron code that reads `location_plans` is untouched). Tests: one-active-tier atomicity (2nd/3rd tier → assert EXACTLY ONE active tier after), add-on additivity + idempotency, validation (location-in-org, active plan, kind match, version-on-plan, cross-org 404), master-only 401/403, default-version resolution, unassign→no active tier, other-locations-unaffected; plus `buildPlanCatalogue` unit tests. Full CI mirror + `next build`. |
| 395 | REPSET-PLATFORM.3 — tenant support access (read-only + act-on-behalf, audited) | **Phase 3 of the Repset platform-architecture work: lets a MASTER "view into" any tenant from the Platform Console to help them, in two modes, audited.** Built ON TOP of the existing master-impersonation mechanism (`src/lib/impersonation.js`) — a support session opens against a tenant ORGANIZATION and REUSES `startImpersonation()` to swap identity/scope to an owner of that org (org_admin > owner-at-a-location; scope-only fallback when the org has no owner profile), so the master sees the tenant's `/portfolio` account home + studios exactly as they would; the active-location cookie is scoped to a location in the org so the portfolio resolves to that tenant deterministically. Cookie is HMAC-SHA-256 signed (Web Crypto, Edge-safe, secret = `SUPPORT_SESSION_SECRET` ‖ `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`) so it is tamper-evident. **Act-on-behalf** = writes allowed but scoped to the tenant via the reused impersonation (all existing IDOR/location guards keep the master inside that org). **Audit** = new **mig `431_support_sessions.sql`** (FILE ONLY — NOT applied; orchestrator applies via MCP): one open row per master (master id, target org id, impersonated user id, mode, reason, ip/ua, started/ended, auto_closed); RLS = master-only SELECT + RESTRICTIVE deny-writes (mig 413/420 shape), service-role writes. Rendered in `AppShell` in place of the plain impersonation banner while a support session is active. **Master-only** throughout: start/switch/exit gate on the REAL underlying master (`impersonatingFrom.masterId ‖ profileRole==='master'`) → 403 otherwise; no new `WEB_PERMISSIONS` key (role-gated like the other master surfaces). Tests: proxy read-only-blocks-writes decision (mutating→403, GET allowed, act_on_behalf allowed, control routes allowed, fail-closed on tamper) + sign/verify round-trip + stale-close planner + cross-tenant target selection. Full CI mirror + `next build`. Migration NOT applied — HELD FOR REVIEW. |

| 291 | SEQ-LOOP-FIX — WhatsApp/SMS sequence steps re-sent every ~10 min (22P02 silent cursor-advance failure) | Live incident (Tim Ivers got the nudge TWICE, 10 min apart): `sendWhatsappStep` returned **Meta's `wamid.…` string** as its send id, but `sequence_enrollments.last_step_send_id` is a **uuid** column → the runner's cursor-advance update was rejected with 22P02 — and the code never checked that update's error, so no error was stamped, the claim lease (10 min) expired, and the tick re-claimed + RE-SENT. Every WhatsApp sequence step would loop like this (email was safe — it returns the `email_sends` uuid; SMS had the same bug via Twilio's `SM…` sid). Fixes: (1) WhatsApp step returns the inserted `whatsapp_messages` row id; SMS step returns its `activities` row id — handlers must return OUR row uuids, never provider ids (3 guard tests). (2) scheduler now **throws when the cursor-advance update errors** → visible `last_error` + 30-min backoff + pause after MAX_ERRORS, instead of an invisible infinite send loop. Residual (noted): a hard crash in the ~100ms between provider-send and cursor-advance can still double-send once per backoff — rare vs tonight's deterministic loop; a per-step idempotency marker is the future hardening if it ever bites. Tim's stuck enrolment was hand-advanced past the send step mid-incident to stop the loop (2 sends total). |
